claim: Neuronopathic Gaucher disease (nGD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic mutations in GBA and buildup of glycosphingolipids in lysosomes.
source: Neuronopathic Gaucher disease (nGD) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic mutations in GBA and buildup of glycosphingolipids in lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information and is supported by established scientific knowledge about Gaucher disease.

claim: In Gaucher disease, biallelic mutations in GBA underlie defective acid β-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase, GCase) and buildup of the primary substrate, glucosylceramide (GluCer), and its inflammatory metabolite glucosylsphingosine (GlcSph) in the lysosomes.
source: In Gaucher disease (GD), biallelic mutations in GBA underlie defective acid β-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase, GCase) and buildup of the primary substrate, glucosylceramide (GluCer), and its inflammatory metabolite glucosylsphingosine (GlcSph) in the lysosomes (Grabowski et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grabowski et al., 2021, indicating it is established knowledge in the field.

claim: GD is classified into three broad phenotypes based on the absence (type 1 GD, GD1) or onset of early-onset neurodegeneration in childhood (fulminant GD type 2, GD2, and slower chronic neurodegeneration, GD3).
source: GD is classified into three broad phenotypes based on the absence (type 1 GD, GD1) or onset of early-onset neurodegeneration in childhood (fulminant GD type 2, GD2, and slower chronic neurodegeneration, GD3).
evidence: This is a standard classification system for Gaucher disease that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Adults with GD1 have a markedly increased risk of Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia (PD/LBD).
source: Adults with GD1 have a markedly increased risk of Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia (PD/LBD) (Bultron et al., 2010; Grabowski et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bultron et al., 2010 and Grabowski et al., 2021.

claim: Heterozygous carriers of GBA mutations are at an increased risk of PD/LBD.
source: Moreover, heterozygous carriers of GBA mutations are at an increased risk of PD/LBD (Aharon-Peretz et al., 2004; Sidransky and Lopez, 2012; Sidransky et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Aharon-Peretz et al., 2004; Sidransky and Lopez, 2012; Sidransky et al., 2009.

claim: Low GCase is reported in the brains of sporadic PD patients who do not harbor GBA mutations.
source: Notably, low GCase is reported in the brains of sporadic PD patients who do not harbor GBA mutations (Gegg et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gegg et al., 2022.

claim: Glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine display potent inflammatory and immunogenic activities.
source: Glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine display potent inflammatory and immunogenic activities (Nagata et al., 2017; Nair et al., 2015; Nair et al., 2016; Pandey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Nagata et al., 2017; Nair et al., 2015; Nair et al., 2016; Pandey et al., 2017.

claim: Treatment of non-neuronopathic GD1 involves enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) targeted to the macrophages via mannose receptors and substrate reduction therapies (SRTs) using inhibitors of glucosylceramide synthase (GCS).
source: Treatment of non-neuronopathic GD1 involves enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) targeted to the macrophages via mannose receptors and substrate reduction therapies (SRTs) using inhibitors of glucosylceramide synthase (GCS) (Cox et al., 2000; Mistry et al., 2017a; Mistry et al., 2017b; Platt et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Cox et al., 2000; Mistry et al., 2017a; Mistry et al., 2017b; Platt et al., 2018.

claim: Currently, there are no effective therapies for the devastating neurodegenerative sequela of GBA mutations.
source: However, currently, there are no effective therapies for the devastating neurodegenerative sequela of GBA mutations.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the introduction, representing current knowledge in the field.

claim: A randomized-controlled trial of brain-penetrant SRT, N-butyldeoxynojirimycin, in patients' GD3 was unsuccessful in ameliorating neurological manifestations.
source: A randomized-controlled trial of brain-penetrant SRT, N-butyldeoxynojirimycin. in patients' GD3 was unsuccessful in ameliorating neurological manifestations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schiffmann et al., 2008.

claim: N-butyldeoxynojirimycin is a relatively weak inhibitor of GCS with significant off-target effects.
source: However, N-butyldeoxynojirimycin is a relatively weak inhibitor of GCS with significant off-target effects (Schiffmann et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schiffmann et al., 2008.

claim: Using a more specific, brain-penetrant GCS inhibitor in a chemically induced model of nGD, some disease pathways were ameliorated on bulk RNA analysis, but had no effect on inflammatory pathways.
source: Using a more specific, brain-penetrant GCS inhibitor in a chemically induced model of nGD, some disease pathways were ameliorated on bulk RNA analysis, but had no effect on inflammatory pathways (Blumenreich et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blumenreich et al., 2021.

claim: Microglia are specialized, self-renewing, CNS-resident macrophages that represent the dominant immune cells involved in maintaining CNS homeostasis.
source: Microglia are specialized, self-renewing, CNS-resident macrophages that represent the dominant immune cells involved in maintaining CNS homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microglia in neuroscience.

claim: Emerging data from single-cell analysis and genome-wide association studies of several neurodegenerative diseases have revealed a central role of microglia in neurodegeneration.
source: Emerging data from single-cell analysis and genome-wide association studies of several neurodegenerative diseases have revealed a central role of microglia in neurodegeneration (Chen and Colonna, 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Colonna, 2021a.

claim: Most studies in GD have focused on GBA deficiency in neurons, while contribution of other cell types in driving the disease pathology has been considered minor.
source: Although several mechanisms have been proposed to explain neurodegeneration associated with GBA mutations, most studies in GD have focused on GBA deficiency in neurons, while contribution of other cell types in driving the disease pathology has been considered minor (Cho et al., 2019; Vitner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2019 and Vitner et al., 2015.

claim: Immunohistochemical evidence of microglial alteration have been reported in neuronopathic GD.
source: Immunohistochemical evidence of microglial alteration have been reported in neuronopathic GD, but the effect of GBA deficiency in microglia per se is not understood.
evidence: This is stated as existing evidence in the field, though the source is not explicitly cited in this sentence.

claim: Gbalsl/lsl mice (loxP-stop-loxP) with a germline deletion of Gba phenocopies human GD2, fulminant neuronopathic GD.
source: Importantly, we used both early-onset neuronopathic GD mice Gbalsl/lsl (loxP-stop-loxP) mice, with a germline deletion of Gba (henceforth referred to as nGD mice) which phenocopies human GD2, fulminant neuronopathic GD (Enquist et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enquist et al., 2007.

claim: Infiltration of CCR2+ macrophages (MFs) defined as CD11bhi CD45+CCR2+ CD64+ TIMD4- population was noted in the nGD brain from an early time point day 2, which showed a steady increase until day 14.
source: Infiltration of CCR2+ macrophages (MFs) defined as CD11bhi CD45+CCR2+ CD64+ TIMD4- population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) was noted in the nGD brain from an early time point day 2, which showed a steady increase until day 14 when the mice reached the humane end point (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was attrition of homeostatic microglia and incremental infiltration of diverse immune cells into nGD brains, which coincided with mice displaying clear signs of neurodegeneration.
source: Concurrently, there was attrition of homeostatic microglia and incremental infiltration of diverse immune cells into nGD brains, which coincided with mice displaying clear signs of neurodegeneration (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Microglia from nGD brains harbored elevated levels of GluCer species (C16, C18, and C20), as well as GlcSph.
source: Microglia from nGD brains harbored elevated levels of GluCer species (C16, C18, and C20), as well as GlcSph.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC/MS/MS data on flow-sorted microglia mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The immune cell infiltrates in the nGD brains were enriched in glucosylceramides (C16 and C18).
source: Notably, the immune cell infiltrates in the nGD brains were also enriched in glucosylceramides (C16 and C18) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: scRNA-seq analysis revealed 15 distinct cellular clusters of CD45+ cells in nGD and control brains.
source: Dimensionality reduction using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) analysis revealed 15 distinct cellular clusters of CD45+ cells (numbered 0–14) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The microglia and immune cell infiltrates in nGD brains exhibited a striking upregulation of type 1 interferon signature genes (ISG).
source: Interestingly, the B cell population (cluster 4) appeared more pronounced in nGD brains, although it was also present in controls. The microglia and immune cell infiltrates in nGD brains exhibited a striking upregulation of type 1 interferon signature genes (ISG) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Microglia of nGD mice exhibited clear downregulation of homeostatic genes and concomitant upregulation of disease-associated microglia (DAM) signature genes, in addition to upregulation of ISGs.
source: Microglia of nGD mice exhibited clear downregulation of homeostatic genes and concomitant upregulation of disease-associated microglia (DAM) signature genes, in addition to upregulation of ISGs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by total RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Restoration of Gba in microglia (nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice) led to more than twofold increase in survival compared to nGD mice.
source: Notably, restoration of Gba in microglia (nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice) led to more than twofold increase in survival compared to nGD mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Selective restoration of Gba in neurons (nGD NesCre/+ mice) further enhanced the survival up to ~200 days.
source: Selective restoration of Gba in neurons (nGD NesCre/+ mice) further enhanced the survival up to ~200 days where they reached the humane end point (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Restoration of Gba in microglia of nGD mice (nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+) resulted in increased homeostatic microglia with reduction in CCR2+ MFs and peripheral immune cell infiltration compared to nGD brains.
source: Restoration of Gba in microglia of nGD mice (nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+) resulted in increased homeostatic microglia with reduction in CCR2+ MFs and peripheral immune cell infiltration compared to nGD brains (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Restoration of Gba in neurons of nGD mice (nGD NesCre/+) blocked attrition of microglia as well as the infiltration of CCR2+ MFs and peripheral immune cells.
source: In contrast, restoration of Gba in neurons of nGD mice (nGD NesCre/+) blocked attrition of microglia as well as the infiltration of CCR2+ MFs and peripheral immune cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Induction of intracellular Pro-IL-1ß in microglia was observed in both nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ brains but not in nGD NesCre/+ brains.
source: Correspondingly, induction of intracellular Pro-IL-1ß in microglia, an indicator of microglial activation, was observed in both nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ brains (Figure 2D and E) but not in nGD NesCre/+ brains (Figure 2D and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, 2E, 2F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice and nGD NesCre/+ mice showed striking reduction of brain glucosylceramides (by ≥90% for C16 and C18:1, and by 50–70% for C18, C20:1, C22, C22.1, C24, and C24:1, and by 38% for C20 glucosylceramide) with a concomitant, striking reduction of GlcSph (89–98%).
source: Consistent with this notion, compared to nGD mice, both nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice and nGD NesCre/+ mice showed striking reduction of brain glucosylceramides (by ≥90% for C16 and C18:1, and by 50–70% for C18, C20:1, C22, C22.1, C24, and C24:1, and by 38% for C20 glucosylceramide) with a concomitant, striking reduction of GlcSph (89–98%, shown in Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ brains showed a pronounced accumulation of GlcSph and several GluCer species (C16, C18, C20, and C22 GluCer species) compared to control brains.
source: Remarkably, Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ brains showed a pronounced accumulation of GlcSph and several GluCer species (C16, C18, C20, and C22 GluCer species) compared to control brains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Aged Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice (~12 months old) started to exhibit motor deficits manifested by a longer time to complete the beam walk and increased tendency to slip.
source: Young mice appeared healthy despite accumulation of GluCer/GlcSph in the brain, but aged Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice (~12 months old) started to exhibit motor deficits manifested by a longer time to complete the beam walk and increased tendency to slip (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text but the supporting data is not shown.

claim: Sera of young Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice (6–8 weeks) showed elevated levels of GlcSph, which tended to increase further in aged (14 months) mice compared to healthy controls.
source: HPLC-MS/MS analysis revealed elevated levels of GlcSph in the sera of young Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice (6–8 weeks), which tended to increase further in aged (14 months) mice compared to healthy controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a significant reduction in microglia and increase in CCR2+ MFs and immune cell infiltration in aged Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice, while no changes were observed in young Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
source: Congruently, there was a significant reduction in microglia and increase in CCR2+ MFs and immune cell infiltration in aged Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice, while no changes were observed in young Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In aged Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ brains, DAM signature clusters (1 and 4), along with the Gba locus-associated gene cluster (cluster 5) and interferon-induced gene cluster (cluster 7), represented the major microglial populations.
source: Notably, in aged Gbafl/fl Cx3cr1Cre/+ brains, DAM signature clusters (1 and 4), along with the Gba locus-associated gene cluster (cluster 5) and interferon-induced gene cluster (cluster 7), represented the major microglial populations (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Aged Gbafl/fl Cx3cr1Cre/+ microglia expressed higher levels of chemokines (Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl2, etc.), inflammatory molecules (Tnf, Il1a, and Il1b), and key DAM signature genes (Apoe, Spp1, Lpl, Ccl3, and Cst7).
source: Aged Gbafl/fl Cx3cr1Cre/+ microglia also expressed higher levels of chemokines (Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl2, etc.), inflammatory molecules (Tnf, Il1a, and Il1b), and key DAM signature genes (Apoe, Spp1, Lpl, Ccl3, and Cst7) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In nGD mouse models with robust neuroinflammation, there was prominent GzmA+ NK cell infiltration.
source: In our nGD mouse models with robust neuroinflammation, we found prominent GzmA+ NK cell infiltration.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Brain-infiltrating NK cells expressed granzyme A (GzmA).
source: We confirmed striking NK infiltration in nGD brains by flow cytometry (Figure 4A–C). Brain-infiltrating NK cells expressed granzyme A (GzmA) (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Higher percentages of NK cell infiltration were observed in nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice brain compared to nGD mice brain.
source: Interestingly, higher percentages of NK cell infiltration were observed in nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice brain compared to nGD mice brain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: NK cell frequency and GzmA expression were unaltered in the spleens of both nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
source: NK cell frequency and GzmA expression were unaltered in the spleens of both nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4G and H), implying that the primary cues responsible for activation of NK cells were emanating from within the nGD brains.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4G and H.

claim: There was no specific buildup of sphingosine lipid species including Sph-1P in nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice brains compared to the control mice.
source: We found no specific buildup of sphingosine lipid species including Sph-1P in nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice brains compared to the control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that other mechanism(s) may underlie NK cell infiltration or that there is local generation of S1P that is beyond the resolution of HPLC-MS/MS.
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Administration of CBE in WT mice resulted in the nGD phenotype.
source: Administration of CBE in WT mice resulted in the nGD phenotype, as described previously (Farfel-Becker et al., 2011; Kanfer et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Farfel-Becker et al., 2011 and Kanfer et al., 1982.

claim: FACS analysis of immune cells in the brains of CBE-treated mice revealed major infiltration of immune cells as well as Pro-IL-1ß induction in the microglia.
source: FACS analysis of immune cells in the brains of CBE-treated mice revealed major infiltration of immune cells (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) as well as Pro-IL-1ß induction in the microglia (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4I, 4J, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Immune cell phenotyping in the brains of CBE-treated mice showed striking induction of GzmA+ NK cells.
source: Like genetic models, immune cell phenotyping in the brains of CBE-treated mice showed striking induction of GzmA+ NK cells (Figure 4K and L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4K, 4L, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lysosomal biology, ISG, and ApoE genes were highly upregulated in microglia, Purkinje, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and neurons in the brains of nGD and 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
source: In the brains of nGD and 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice both with overt neurodegenerative phenotypes, lysosomal biology, ISG, and ApoE genes were highly upregulated in microglia, Purkinje, oligodendrocytes (clusters 2, 34, and 36), astrocytes (clusters 22, 23, 4, 48, 52, and 9), and neurons (0, 3, 5, and 6) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Microglia of 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice were similar to controls.
source: In contrast, microglia of 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice were similar to controls.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DAM markers were significantly enriched in microglia from both nGD and 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ compared to 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
source: In line with these observations, DAM markers were significantly enriched in microglia from both nGD and 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ compared to 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), consolidating the importance of microglial Gba in ameliorating neurodegeneration seen in florid acute neuroinflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Gba rescue in the neuronal compartment resulted in the normalization of pathways associated with lysosomal biology genes, ISG genes, chemokine genes, and ApoE in microglia, Purkinje, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and neuron cell clusters.
source: Gba rescue in the neuronal compartment resulted in the normalization of pathways associated with lysosomal biology genes, ISG genes, chemokine genes, and ApoE in microglia, Purkinje, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and neuron cell clusters, and in other brain cell clusters (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: nGD mice exhibited the largest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (n = 19,274), which were strikingly reduced in 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ (n = 125) and also in nGD NesCre/+ brains, n = 256.
source: Gene expression analysis revealed that nGD mice exhibited the largest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (n = 19,274), which were strikingly reduced in 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ (n = 125) and also in nGD NesCre/+ brains, n = 256 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DAA genes were highly induced in astrocyte clusters from nGD mice and in 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice but not in 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
source: DAA genes were highly induced in astrocyte clusters from nGD mice and in 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice but not in 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: IPA revealed enrichment of necroptosis, interferon, IL8, TREM1, and neuroinflammation signaling pathways in 2-week-old nGD mice compared to the controls.
source: IPA revealed enrichment of necroptosis, interferon, IL8, TREM1, and neuroinflammation signaling pathways in 2-week-old nGD mice compared to the controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Gba rescue in microglia of 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice showed abrogation of neuroinflammatory pathways seen in nGD brains.
source: Gba rescue in microglia of 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice showed abrogation of neuroinflammatory pathways seen in nGD brains (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Both interferon and NK cell signaling pathways were upregulated in 2-week-old nGD and in 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ brains.
source: Notably, both interferon and NK cell signaling pathways were upregulated in 2-week-old nGD and in 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ brains (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Astrocytes from nGD mice showed higher fluorescence after treatment with CellROX, indicating a higher level of ROS, compared to astrocytes from control mice.
source: Consistent with the transcriptional changes observed in nGD mice, astrocytes from nGD mice showed higher fluorescence after treatment with CellROX, indicating a higher level of ROS, compared to astrocytes from control mice (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: nGD astrocytes with high ROS level also showed elevated accumulation of neutral lipids, as seen by BODIPY staining.
source: nGD astrocytes with high ROS level also showed elevated accumulation of neutral lipids, as seen by BODIPY staining (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Activated microglia in the nGD brain showed enhanced ROS level along with an increased accumulation of lipids compared to homeostatic microglia.
source: Moreover, activated microglia in the nGD brain showed enhanced ROS level along with an increased accumulation of lipids compared to homeostatic microglia (Figure 5I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: GZ-161 treatment significantly prolonged the survival of nGD mice.
source: Consistent with previous studies, GZ-161 treatment significantly prolonged the survival of nGD mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GZ-161 treatment of nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice resulted in considerable extension of survival compared to untreated mice, with analogous normalization of GlcSph levels in the sera of treated nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
source: Indeed, GZ-161 treatment of nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice resulted in considerable extension of survival compared to untreated mice, with analogous normalization of GlcSph levels in the sera of treated nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data and lipidomics data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: GZ-161 treatment significantly reduced the proportion of CCR2+ MFs, concomitantly with restoration of homeostatic microglia compartment in nGD mice.
source: FACS analysis of GZ-161-treated nGD mice showed that the GCS inhibitor significantly reduced the proportion of CCR2+ MFs, concomitantly with restoration of homeostatic microglia compartment (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: GZ-161 treatment had no effect on immune cell infiltrates in the brains of nGD mice.
source: However, GZ-161 treatment had no effect on immune cell infiltrates in the brains of nGD mice (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: GZ-161 treatment in nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice resulted in a reduction in Pro-IL-1ß+ microglia as well as a reduction in GzmA+ immune cells in the brain.
source: GZ-161 treatment in longer-lived nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice wherein drug administration was more reliable resulted in significantly increased survival (Figure 6A) accompanied by a reduction in Pro-IL-1ß+ microglia as well as a reduction in GzmA+ immune cells in the brain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6F and G.

claim: Administration of GZ-161 in CBE-treated mice reduced infiltration of NK cells in the brain.
source: We further evaluated the ability of GZ-161 to counteract NK cell induction seen in the CBE model. Administration of GZ-161 in CBE-treated mice reduced infiltration of NK cells in the brain (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice accumulated HexCer (d18:1/18:0) and HexCer (d18:1/20:0) in the corpus callosum, which was normalized upon GZ-161 diet.
source: Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice accumulated HexCer (d18:1/18:0) and HexCer (d18:1/20:0) in the corpus callosum (Figure 7A), which was normalized upon GZ-161 diet.
evidence: This claim is supported by MALDI imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was a reduction in HexCer (18:1/22:0) accumulation in the cerebral cortex of Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice upon GZ-161 treatment.
source: Concomitantly, there was a reduction in HexCer (18:1/22:0) accumulation in the cerebral cortex (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MALDI imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: DAM cluster 2, which was significantly enriched in Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ brains, was markedly reduced in Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice fed with GZ-161 diet with concurrent enhancement of homeostatic microglia clusters 0 and 1.
source: DAM cluster 2, which was significantly enriched in Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ brains, was markedly reduced in Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice fed with GZ-161 diet with concurrent enhancement of homeostatic microglia clusters 0 and 1 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: GZ-161 treatment resulted in reduction of Gzma, Ccl5, Tyrobp, and Klf2 in NK cells, with no change in Klrd1, Klrk1, CD52, and Ccl4.
source: GZ-161 treatment resulted in reduction of Gzma, Ccl5, Tyrobp, and Klf2, with no change in Klrd1, Klrk1, CD52, and Ccl4 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: There was a massive 2000-fold elevation of serum Nf-L in nGD mice, ~100-fold elevation in nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+, and ~20-fold elevation in nGD NesCre/+ mice.
source: Using ultra-sensitive Quanterix Simoa, we found a massive 2000-fold elevation of serum Nf-L in nGD mice, ~100-fold elevation in nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+, and ~20-fold elevation in nGD NesCre/+ mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nf-L measurement data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: GZ-161 treatment led to a significant decline in serum Nf-L levels in nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
source: Remarkably, GZ-161 treatment, which led to reductions in GlcSph levels, also led to a significant decline in serum Nf-L levels in nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nf-L measurement data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Serum Nf-L level in nGD mice (18,100 ± 4809 pg/ml) was reduced by GZ-161 treatment to 6876 ± 1080 pg/ml.
source: Serum Nf-L level in nGD mice (18,100 ± 4809 pg/ml) was reduced by GZ-161 treatment to 6876 ± 1080 pg/ml.
evidence: This claim is supported by Nf-L measurement data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: GZ-161 treatment of nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice dramatically reduced Nf-L level to 1297 ± 534.1 pg/ml compared to untreated mice (5466 ± 557.2 pg/ml).
